body:
confirmed PostgreSQL doesn't want to assume "public" for the non-qualified table, which is unfortunate.

this is a very unusual use case and you certainly can schema-qualify tables as public, just set up the mapping as such and your MCVE (works perfectly, thanks) works fine

```py
from sqlalchemy import Column, create_engine, ForeignKey, Integer
from sqlalchemy.engine.url import URL
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship
from sqlalchemy.orm.session import sessionmaker

Base = declarative_base()


class Foo(Base):
    __tablename__ = "foo"
    __table_args__ = dict(schema="foo")

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)


class Bar(Base):
    __tablename__ = "foo"
    __table_args__ = dict(schema="public")

    id = Column(ForeignKey("foo.foo.id"), primary_key=True)

    foo = relationship("Foo", uselist=False)


engine = create_engine(
    "postgresql://scott:tiger@localhost/test", echo='debug'
)


engine.execute("drop schema if exists foo cascade")
engine.execute("create schema foo")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
Session = sessionmaker()
session = Session(bind=engine)

session.query(Bar).join(Foo).all()
```

body: I think this may be uncommon enough that the solution could be to qualify the schema in both tables
good news, the behavior can be reproduced with any schema name, it's just the two tables in same schema that have the problem, which eases testing burden.   can target this sooner as a result.

this is a weird one because this issue has existed literally for 16 years, and while we have had a lot of funny name-conflict kinds of issues reported, never this one.   so we would assume this is *extremely* unlikely.

but from there it's all somewhat bad news.  The workaround of schema-qualifying the table is not database agnostic, because the "default schema name" is different for every database.   The upcoming gerrit illustrates a fix for this problem, which adds a small expense to the compilation of statements in order to track these names up front to identfy conflicts; we have to add this as a separate step because we render columns clauses and WHERE clauses before we render FROM clauses.    We do already have a scan for "FROM" objects up front for SELECT / UPDATE / DELETE but it has to traverse joins for this; it's negligible overhead and it's cached.

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**track item schema names to identify name collisions w/ default schema** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3412

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_1_4** branch:

**track item schema names to identify name collisions w/ default schema** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3413
the overhead is really small but the ratio of CPU cycles to actual need is still going to be extremely massive

alrighty:

works for PG, MySQL and SQLite.

SQL Server: "sqlalchemy.exc.ProgrammingError: (pyodbc.ProgrammingError) ('42000', '[42000] [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server][SQL Server]The objects "test_schema.some_table" and "some_table" in the FROM clause have the same exposed names. Use correlation names to distinguish them. (1013) (SQLExecDirectW)')"   forget it.   we're not doing that

Oracle: it's having some problem creating the tables, need to check if Oracle has a restriction on cross-schema FKs which it shouldnt

don't know the syntax for Oracle because I dont know what the "implicit" schema name is.  the default schema name is the username for that DB but we can't qualify with that, it's rejecting that name.

so for now this is a fix for the OSS backends only, Oracle/SQL Server are excluded.  PostgreSQL is the only database where people really use schemas a lot.

well anyway, SQL Server's error message leads us to the other workaround here, which is just use an alias:

```py
f1 = aliased(Foo)

session.query(Bar).join(f1).all()
```

automatically aliasing that is a huge rabbit hole that we've been actually trying to pull out of in 2.0.

overall the best fix for this issue is to just not name your tables that way.

oh the fix also won't work reliably for PostgreSQL if you have multiple entries in search_path and the table is not against the first entry.   we get search_path from current_schema().  "current_schema returns the name of the schema that is first in the search path (or a null value if the search path is empty). This is the schema that will be used for any tables or other named objects that are created without specifying a target schema."

to add automatic aliasing into the compiler, rather than at the SQL construction level which is where we've historically done this (the whole adapt() thing), is somewhat doable but it would add a burden to all table rendering everywhere, that this additional context has to be passed through and checked in the same way we do for columns etc., it would be all over the place.  doesn't feel worth it yet though it would be more consistent for how we alias same-named columns.
